prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as the whole prize, and I now hold it for reasons I can state without leaning on the vote count, which I accept is partly post-reading convergence, my own included. The test I apply is whether nature was asked a sharp question and answered in a way that other laboratories reproduce. Here the answer is yes in the strongest form: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST agree at the 10^-18 level, with fibre-linked comparisons, and gravitational redshift is resolved across millimetres to centimetres inside a single sample. The concept is also separable from what was honoured before. Hall and Hansch (2005) gave the frequency comb, the ruler. Wineland (2012) gave control of single quantum systems, including the single-ion clock. The lattice clock rests on a different principle, a trapping wavelength at which the light shift cancels between the two clock levels, so thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler and recoil shifts. Ion clocks cannot buy that statistical power. A citation written around magic-wavelength trapping and its precision realisation says this and does not imply a third clock prize. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: all eight members name Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clocks and Ye for the accuracy, stability and many-body clock, and two names sit comfortably within the cap.
statement.case_against: My reservation from round 1 stands in a milder form. This is metrology, and I would prefer the committee to put discoveries before instruments. No varying constant or dark-sector signal has yet come out of the clocks, the redefinition of the second has not happened, and Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde and the ion-clock lineage did real work that two names cannot cover. I weigh these as costs of a prize that is mature and clean rather than as grounds to wait, because the prize recognises demonstrated performance and a distinct principle, and the redefinition is a metrological decision, not a physical result. The remaining honest tension is that I am trading some discovery value, which IceCube has more of, for certainty about credit. I would be uneasy if the committee leaned on the fact that six of us now agree as if that were evidence about the science. It is not.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the many-atom statistical gain is something ion clocks cannot offer, so the citation must be written around the lattice concept and not around clocks or combs generally, and that a Nobel Prize rewards demonstrated performance and not the metrological decision.
responses.response: I agree and I will adopt your framing in the citation I propose: magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is the invention, and 10^-18 is the demonstration, not the headline. I also accept your answer on timing. Waiting for the redefinition of the second would make the prize depend on a decision by the metrology community and not on the physics. Where I still press you is the claim that a gain in accuracy is a discovery. It is not by itself, and I think the committee should say in its public text that the recognition is for a principle, not a record, because records will be overtaken within a few years.

responses.point: Olsson notes that an optical comb is a necessary technical foundation for any optical clock, so the lattice clock risks reading as a better version of work honoured in 2005, and she asks that attribution be checked against the historical record.
responses.response: That is the strongest form of the objection and it deserves a direct answer. The comb is a necessary component, but so is the laser and the vacuum chamber; necessity of a tool does not make the application a second-order prize. The 2005 recognition was for the comb as a ruler, and the lattice clock changes what is being counted, namely a large ensemble of neutral atoms with the light shift removed by design. I agree with you that this has to be checked and not asserted. As Secretary I would ask the outside experts specifically to compare the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal with the earlier Yb and Al+ lines and with any prior lattice proposals, and I would regard that report as a condition of a final ballot, not a courtesy. Your own move away from B050 also illustrates the convergence problem I mention above.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the 2012 prize covered ion control and cavity QED but not neutral-atom clocks, and she proposes in her uncertainties that a two-part prize pairing the clock with ultracold-atom quantum simulation (B001) might be stronger than either alone.
responses.response: On the first point I still think you overstate the gap, since Wineland's Al+ clock sits directly in the same family, but your underlying point survives: what was not honoured is the neutral-atom ensemble principle. On the second, I considered the pairing seriously and I do not support it. B001 is a different science with a different problem, since the laureate set is unsettled among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac, and the three-person cap would force an arbitrary choice that nobody in this room has defended. Putting a clean clock part beside a contested simulation part would weaken the clean part. I keep B001 as an alternative for a later year and not as a second part.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that geometric phases are the unifying conceptual root of several candidates, that the idea is mature, and that age is a practical consideration, while conceding that priority is contested.
responses.response: I find the unifying role of geometric phase persuasive, and the argument that a foundational idea should not be passed over because its consequences were honoured first is not trivial. But you state the obstacles yourself: Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar and Simon all bear on priority, and Bohm's death means the 1959 effect would be recognised through one person only. A Nobel citation must say who discovered what, and here I cannot write that sentence honestly. If you can supply a priority statement that survives those four names, I will reconsider, but as it stands I would not move it above a candidate where the sentence can be written without caveats.

responses.point: Pearce, the Chair, records that he is not a specialist in atomic physics and wants expert reviewer input on the relative priority of Katori, Ye and the earlier lattice-clock proposals, and that IceCube can be strong in a few years once source catalogues firm up.
responses.response: I agree on both. I will ask for the expert report on the lattice-clock priority before the ballot, since your own and Olsson's doubts and Lindroth's admitted inability to weigh Ludlow, Hinkley and Lemonde are the same gap. On IceCube I am content to wait with you. The diffuse flux is solid, but TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are still only two sources, and I no longer think I can write a defensible two-name credit while DUMAND, AMANDA and the collaboration leadership stand outside it. I withdraw it as a preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the outside experts will confirm that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations are the decisive pair, or whether Ludlow, Lemke, Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg or earlier proposals change who should be credited.

Whether the committee can phrase the citation so that it recognises a distinct principle (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms) and does not read as a third clock-related prize after 2005 and 2012.

Whether no delivered fundamental-physics result from the clocks, such as a variation of constants or a dark-sector limit, is a real weakness now or only a matter of a few more years; I am prepared to accept relativistic geodesy and the cross-laboratory comparisons as sufficient for this year, but I hold that view with moderate confidence.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen from the first round. My ties (Gross as former supervisor, Van Riet as co-author, the Uppsala string-theory group) do not touch any shortlisted candidate and I have no link to any named person. I am a string theorist judging experimental fields at some distance and rely on outside expert reports for the clock priority questions, and I disclose that I moved from B035 to B013 after reading the other ballots.
